10od2uf:364: . These two sentences capture the essential difference between the two types of automation. Traditional software automation relies on the explicit formalization of rules—you must be able to precisely write business logic as code. LLM automation, on the other hand, relies on verifiability—you don't need to write out rules, but you must be able to judge whether the output is right or wrong. This framework explains why LLM capabilities surge in domains like math and code, which have clear verification standards, but fail on tasks like the "car wash problem"—which humans find simple but cannot be structurally verified. It also explains the "jagged intelligence" phenomenon of LLMs. The capability distribution is not smooth, but depends on which verifiable domains RL training has covered. If a domain can be constructed with a large number of reinforcement learning samples, the model can quickly reach expert level; if it falls outside the data distribution, the model will make mistakes even on things that humans consider common sense. The leap in chess ability from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 was not because "the model became smarter overall," but because someone at OpenAI decided to add chess data to pretraining.

xr2kxr:293: Karpathy uses "ghost" to describe LLMs, pushing back against a common anthropomorphic misuse: treating an LLM like an animal — yelling at it makes it afraid, praising it sparks intrinsic motivation. In reality, LLMs have neither emotions nor intrinsic motivation; their behavior comes entirely from statistical simulation, context, tool calls, and the reward mechanisms used in training. This framework has direct practical implications: don't waste emotions on models; optimize context and reward signals instead. Karpathy says he no longer remembers API details among PyTorch, NumPy, and pandas (models remember them better than he does), but he still must understand the underlying concepts — what a tensor is, the relationship between view and storage, and when data gets copied.
